blocks.text: A company sells one flange in eight bore sizes. Changing one dimension in the model should resize the flange, the bolt circle and the hole pattern; if it instead produces red rebuild errors, the model was built without design intent.

blocks.markdown: A parametric model is a recipe, not a shape: each feature is rebuilt, in order, from its sketch dimensions and relations. **Design intent** is the reason behind those numbers: which dimensions are the real requirements (a bore for a particular shaft), and which follow from them (an outer diameter that is always 2.2 times the bore). A model that captures intent can be edited in one place and update everywhere; a model that records only the present geometry breaks when you touch it.

blocks.title: Design intent
blocks.text: **Design intent** is the set of relationships a model must keep when a dimension changes. It is captured by choosing a few **key (driving) dimensions**, expressing other sizes as **equations** of them, and attaching features to stable references such as planes and the origin.

blocks.caption: Example equations for a flange: d is the bore diameter (mm, the key parameter), D the outer diameter, t the thickness, PCD the bolt-circle diameter

blocks.title: A flange driven by the bore
blocks.prompt: A flange has bore diameter d = 40 mm and the equations above. Compute D, t and PCD, then repeat for d = 60 mm.

steps.text: Substitute d = 40 mm into each equation.
The bolt circle is the mean of bore and outer diameters.

blocks.answer: d = 40: D = 88, t = 10, PCD = 64 mm. d = 60: D = 132, t = 15, PCD = 96 mm. Only one number was edited.

blocks.markdown: Models fail to rebuild when a feature loses something it depended on. Common causes: **dimensioning to an edge or face created by a fillet or chamfer** (which may disappear when sizes change), **fillet or chamfer sizes that are fixed numbers** (which can exceed the geometry), **sketching on a face that is later removed or re-created**, **cyclic equations** (two dimensions each defined in terms of the other), and **references to a later feature**. Robust models reference planes and the origin, add fillets last, and size them by equation.

rows: The edge disappears if the radius changes
Dimension to the original sharp edge or a plane
Fails when the face becomes narrower than 2R
Set R as a fraction of the width, for example 0.4 w
Sketch on a face of a feature
Face is lost if that feature is edited
Two equations that define each other
One driving dimension, the other driven
blocks.caption: Typical rebuild failures and fixes

blocks.title: A fillet that cannot fit
blocks.prompt: A rib face is w = 10 mm wide and carries a fillet of fixed radius R = 6 mm on each of its two long edges. Why does the rebuild fail, and what equation makes it robust?

steps.text: Two fillets on one face consume 2R of its width.
The face is only 10 mm wide, so 12 mm > 10 mm: the fillets overlap and the solver cannot form the geometry.
Replace the fixed radius by R = 0.4 w. Then 2R = 0.8 w, which is always less than w.

blocks.answer: A fixed 6 mm radius fails since 12 mm > 10 mm; R = 0.4 w gives 4 mm and stays valid for every w.

blocks.markdown: A **configuration** (also called a variant or family-table entry) stores a named set of parameter values and suppression states for the same part file. A flange for bores of 25 mm and 40 mm is one model with two configurations, not two files, so geometry fixes apply to both. Each configuration changes only the key parameters; the equations compute the rest.

blocks.caption: Two configurations of one part from the same equations

blocks.title: Avoid circular equations
blocks.text: If d = D/2.2 and D = 2.2 d are both written, the solver cannot decide which drives which. Choose one driving dimension and make the others driven.

items: Choose the few dimensions that express the real requirement.
Write all other sizes as equations of those dimensions.
Reference planes and the origin, not fragile edges.
Add fillets and chamfers last, sized by equation.
Test by changing each key value across its full range.

points: Design intent means choosing key dimensions and expressing everything else as equations of them.
Rebuild failures come from fragile references, fixed sizes that stop fitting, and circular equations.
A configuration stores two or more sizes of one model by changing only the key parameters.

questions.stem: In the equation D = 2.2 d for a flange, which dimension is the driving (key) dimension?

distractorRationale.d: One of them has to drive.

questions.explanation: The equation computes D from d, so d is the value the designer edits. D becomes a driven dimension and must not also be typed in.

questions.stem: Which modelling habit most commonly causes a rebuild failure when a dimension is changed?

options.text: Dimensioning to the edge created by a fillet
Using the origin as a reference

questions.correctOptionText: Dimensioning to the edge created by a fillet
questions.explanation: A fillet edge can vanish or move when sizes change, so features attached to it lose their reference. Referencing the origin and using equations are good practice.

questions.stem: A flange is built with D = 2.2 d and bolt-circle diameter PCD = (d + D)/2, where d is the bore. For a bore d = 25 mm, calculate the PCD in mm.
questions.explanation: D = 2.2 x 25 = 55 mm, so PCD = (25 + 55)/2 = 40 mm. Equation-driven models avoid recalculating this by hand.

questions.stem: A shaft model uses the simplified rule b = d/4 for key width, where d is the shaft diameter (this is a teaching rule, not the standard key table). Calculate the key width b in mm for the configuration d = 32 mm.
questions.explanation: Substituting d = 32 mm gives b = 32/4 = 8 mm. A configuration only needs the value of d to produce this.

questions.stem: Which is the main advantage of using configurations of one part rather than separate files for two sizes?

options.text: A change to the shared feature logic fixes both sizes at once

questions.correctOptionText: A change to the shared feature logic fixes both sizes at once
questions.explanation: All configurations share one feature tree, so corrections propagate. File size or drawing dimensions are not the reason.

questions.stem: A plate carries two fillets of fixed radius 8 mm on one 14 mm wide face. What happens at rebuild, and why?

options.text: It fails because 2 x 8 = 16 mm exceeds 14 mm
It fails because fillets cannot be used on plates
It rebuilds with the fillet ignored

questions.correctOptionText: It fails because 2 x 8 = 16 mm exceeds 14 mm

distractorRationale.a: Each radius alone fits but the two together do not.
distractorRationale.d: The solver errors rather than ignoring the feature.

questions.explanation: The two fillets together need 16 mm of face width but only 14 mm exists. Sizing the radius by an equation would prevent the failure.

questions.stem: A designer enters d = D/2.2 and D = 2.2 d as two separate equations in one sketch. What is the consequence?

options.text: A circular definition that the solver cannot resolve
d and D are always equal
Nothing, the second equation is ignored

questions.correctOptionText: A circular definition that the solver cannot resolve

distractorRationale.c: They are related by 2.2, not equal.

questions.explanation: Each value is defined by the other and nothing fixes either, so the system is circular. One should be the driving dimension.

questions.stem: Name three modelling choices that make a part fail to rebuild when a dimension is changed, and give a robust alternative for each.
markingGuide: Dimension to fillet/chamfer edge: use original edge or plane
Fixed fillet size that stops fitting: size by equation
Sketch on a face of a feature that may be edited: use a datum plane
Circular equation or reference to a later feature: single driving dimension, correct order
questions.explanation: Each answer should pair a cause of failure with a concrete robust practice, such as referencing planes instead of faces. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A bearing housing is made in three sizes, with bore 20, 30 and 45 mm. Describe how you would build one model that produces all three, naming the key parameter, two equations and the configuration set-up.
markingGuide: Equations for outer diameter, wall thickness, bolt circle as functions of d
Create three configurations changing only d to 20, 30, 45
Test each configuration for rebuild errors
questions.explanation: The answer must make one driving dimension and use equations and configurations so only the key value differs between sizes. Each point in the marking guide earns credit, so state every point explicitly and give its reason.

questions.stem: A configuration of a part can change dimension values and which features are suppressed.
questions.explanation: A configuration stores parameter values and suppression states for the same feature tree. This is how one model gives several sizes or variants.
